approaches.name: CAPI, alternative collection methods and modelled welfare indicators for Pacific statistics
approaches.description: Uses CAPI, experimental survey methods, satellite and administrative data, crowdsourcing and phone follow-ups to modernize Pacific household survey data collection. Practices: CAPI replacing paper questionnaires in Pacific household surveys; Alternative data collection methods experimentation component; Harmonization Advisor to build regionally comparable micro-datasets; Harmonized welfare indicators populating Pacific Data Hub portal; Trials of alternative data collection methods with NSOs; Satellite and administrative data models for annual indicator estimates; Crowdsourcing and field enumeration for near real-time indicators; Resident enumerators with CAPI for remote citizenry monitoring; Long-form census module with small area estimation for HIES; Satellite imagery welfare estimation for Pacific islands; Cell-phone follow-up surveys of household survey respondents; Roving supervisors uploading resident enumerator data via sea links.

evidence.text: In addition, integrating new technology, such as Computer-assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI), reduces the need to print and transport paper questionnaires, which has decreased the costs of data collection in certain contexts despite the up-front cost of hardware investment.

extra_evidence.text: However, these issues are compounded by outdated methodologies and inefficient use of technology.

The SPC project will provide US$4.4 million equivalent in grant financing to SPC-SDD across three components: (1) Support to the PSMB (US$1.13 million equivalent), (2) Institutional Strengthening and Implementation Support (US$1.70 million equivalent), and (3) Alternative Data Collection Methods (US$1.57 million equivalent).

Page 15 of 52 The World Bank Statistical Innovation and Capacity Building in the Pacific Islands (P168122) PDO Level Indicators (a) Number of PSMB-commissioned guidance notes approved and disseminated (b) Number of experiment reports produced and submitted to PSMB (c) Number of regionally comparable indicators published on SPC platforms (d) Number of harmonized micro-datasets published on SPC platforms B.

In addition to the two long-term consultants, a medium-term consultant, a Harmonization Advisor, will be hired under Component 2 to initiate microdata harmonization processes to facilitate the production of comparable welfare statistics.
To promote greater access, the project will fund a Harmonization Advisor, a long-term consultant, to develop a set of comparable indicators from these datasets to populate the new Pacific Data Hub.

The Harmonization Advisor will also produce guidelines, covering topics such as harmonization and anonymization, for SPC-SDD to ensure that indicators from newly collected data can be added to the data portal.
For those surveys which SPC-SDD has permission to disseminate, the Harmonization Advisor will construct harmonized micro-datasets for dissemination.

SPC-SDD will work with NSOs in IDA-eligible beneficiary countries, as agreed with the World Bank, to trial alternative data collection methods, based on what is deemed appropriate and most impactful for the specific contexts.

This component includes financing for (a) the costs of developing the experiments, (b) the costs of implementing the experiments, and (c) the costs associated with preparing the analytical reports, submitting them for PSMB review, and broadly disseminating the results across the Pacific.

There are several innovations in data collection that could potentially reduce the costs and complexity of collecting socioeconomic data in PICs, particularly by addressing the vast geography and sparse population constraints to traditional data collection.

For example, combining HIES and census into a long-form census conducted every five years, and then leveraging the cost savings to do annual estimates of key indicators with models built with satellite and administrative data, would increase information for policy makers while still lowering overall costs.
The innovations agenda targets collecting policy-relevant information in nontraditional ways, which could potentially reduce the need for or replace the current HIES system.

Similarly, crowdsourcing and field-based enumeration is inexpensive compared to traditional surveying and can provide near real-time information on certain indicators, if data quality issues can be adequately addressed.

Based on Iterative Beneficiary Monitoring (IBM) systems developed in Africa to collect basic community-level information that can be used to assess well-being, RCM would rely on resident enumerators and electronic data capture.
These responses are then submitted electronically using CAPI software.
RCM would differ to IBM in that some questions would be asked consistently and periodically (price data, for example) rather than a changing set of questions.
Given the high transportation and travel-associated costs of implementing HIES across remote islands, a potential approach to reducing the cost of HIES would be to merge HIES with the census.

This model, which administers a detailed questionnaire to a small subset of census respondents and then uses small area estimation to extrapolate to the wider population, is used in many places in the developed world (including the United States).
The most basic use of satellite data would be as an alternative to traditional household listing.

Promising results deriving well-being estimates from satellite imagery have been demonstrated within the World Bank (research on Sri Lanka and Mexico) and externally (Marshall Burke from Stanford University, among others, has worked in several countries in Africa).
Poverty estimation methods are highly context specific, however, and little work has been done in the Pacific region.
Another possibility would be to collect telephone numbers from respondents in household surveys, and then to follow up with regular phone calls to conduct short interviews on certain subjects.

This model has been demonstrated to be an effective monitoring tool in several contexts (Listening to LAC, Listening to Africa, Listening to Tajikistan) as well as a valuable tool in crisis Page 49 of 52 The World Bank Statistical Innovation and Capacity Building in the Pacific Islands (P168122) situations (cell phone surveys in Sierra Leone and Liberia during the Ebola crisis and for displaced persons in northern Mali).
The main benefit of this method is that it collects data from a random selection of households across the country and can be linked to the baseline data from the household survey.
Given the lack of cell phone coverage in some parts of the Pacific region, a hybrid approach of the ‘Listening to…’ or IBM models may be more appropriate.
One alternative would be to have roving supervisors who traveled by sea links (either passenger ferries or regular cargo ships).
These supervisors would upload the data collected by the resident enumerator in the previous period, download a new set of questions, and pay the enumerator.
